sections.title: Praefatio ad sanctos Patres Tridentinae Synodi

texts.content: UTINAM hoc ab Aquilone excitatum incendium sacrosancta oecumenica, et usquequaque legitima Tridentina Synodus, non violentius ac periculosius Ecclesiam Dei pervasisset, quam cui facile iam sit occursum iri. Non enim tunc adeo me temere in medium proripuissem, quoad meam mecum reputassem inopiam, tenuitatem consuluissem, quid denique ferre valerent humeri, habuissem exploratum. At cum tot iam ex partibus conflagrare Christianorum orbem^[*Lutheranorum incendium late patet.*] attoniti conspiciamus, tamque inde multas dissiluisse scintillas, ut vix fiat reliquus angulus ullus, qui non iamiam flammam accepturus effumet, nihil sane aliud quam operaepretium duxerim, si citra delectum pro sua quisque virili, et quo fuerit divinitus talento donatus, vel tumultuario obviam properantes, opem feramus omnes, ut si qua parte hominum iam medullas exedit, ac cinefecit corda, illud restinguere non sufficimus, saltem ne latius emicare, scintillareque pergat, demum operam. Hi vel maxime qui de hac re conscripti huc sumus. In hoc enim meam etiam exiguitatem ad vos Patres sanctissimi destinauit Caesar, si quod vobis forte qualecunque obsequium possem impendere. Quod si, ut summo iure Christiani tenentur, ita huius sacri ordinis dicto audientes omnes essent, satis nimirum haberent, consulta vestra sanctissima audisse, quibus obedienter parerent. Nam quid est, quod oecumenico concilio, legitime, tum indicto, tum congregato obiectari queat? Ubi secundum Spiritum sanctum tres ex primoribus sacri senatus reverendissimi legati praesident, digni equidem, qui vices Vicarii CHRISTI fungantur. Quibus duo quoque alii eiusdem ordinis Cardinales, et clarissimi et iidem sapientissimi assident. Quo Christianorum principes, cum sanctis antistitibus, oratores etiam suos delegarunt. Quo denique terrarum undique cuiusque gradus ac dignitatis ecclesiasticae iustissimus ac consultissimus coactus est numerus. At vero est inter Patriarchae illius Lutheri errores hic unus^[*Lutheri error.*], omnium causa et fomentum, universorumque adeo pestilentissimus, ut nullum definiendis terminandisque fidei controversiis publicum iudicem admittat, cuius sit auctoritati et iudicio ab omnibus Christianis auscultandum. Iisque Lutheranis eousque insedit animis, ut post triginta annos induciis, conventibus et colloquiis cum eis insumptos, animos iam modo, antequam in concilio compararent, desponderint, infandaque arma sumpserint^[*Lutheranorum arma.*], contra parentem patriae sacram Maiestatem, contra Ecclesiam Dei, contra veritatem Evangelii. Videte proh dolor, spectatissimi Patres, quo unius hominis obstinata caecitas tandem evaserit. Et quod maius est, magisque indolendum miraculum, nunquam^[*Lutherani non adeo potentes.*] errores ulli tam tenues, exilesque seu vitae sanctimoniam, seu doctrinam spectetis, progenitores et patronos habuere. Quoniam neque ovina saltem pelle obtecti, neque ita multum arte instructi. Et tamen ut nulli unquam in perniciem magis Christianae Reipublicae extiterunt, nulli minori negocio tam late diffusi sunt, tamque animos non modo indoctae plebis, verum procerum et principum occuparunt Germanorum: revera gentis, cum rebus clare gestis toto orbe celebratissimae, tum etiam, si non hanc plagam accepissent, religionis sanctimonia Christianissimae. Nisi miraculum non est, ubi tam est in promptu naturalis causa?^[*Haeresum causae.*] Docent licere, quod lubet. At fratres admonere institui, non irritare: nam caritas non agit perperam. Quos eodem mecum sanguine regenuit CHRISTUS, eadem omnes caritate amplector. Veritatem Evangelicam aliis congratulor, quod agnoscant: aliis, ut non diutius ignorent, opto, a Deoque immortali imprecor. Eo praesertim, quod utinam nostri non fuissent perditi mores, legumque dissipationes, unde occasionem isti nacti sunt tantae discessionis. Etenim quae res navigium Petri in has adegit caucates, nostrorum est malorum procella. Et nisi hanc prius sedatam curemus, ne quicquam Patres amplissimi rerum, quam patimur perturbationem, componere, et quibus iactamur haeresum fluctus compescere nitimini. Tametsi potuissent adversarii personarum errata citra iniuriam publicae fidei taxare. Qualescunque enim fuerint privatorum hominum mores, legumque abusus, tamen veritas fidei, omni procul dubio vera est. Nam divina, firmaque adeo et sancta est, et cui ullo ex odio, vel praetextu contraire, nefandum impietatis scelus est. Quo ergo ad initium, unde digressus sum, redeam, nequaquam non quinque ego talenta, nec revera duo acceperim, quae amplius usuris (iuxta Evangelium) duplicare valeam: at tanta mihi visa est horum temporum necessitas, ut meticulus me nonnihil commovere coeperit, ne forte vel unum, quod secundum meam tenuem virtutem receperim, in terram iam nunc defodiam, quod nequitiae mihi detur in die domini. Hanc ob rem post tam multos, eosdemque praeclaros viros, qui a nobis hos annos triginta cum istis feliciter conflixere, opusculum ego hoc de natura et gratia adornabam^[*Nomen operis.*]: meditatus si quid forte mea valeret opera in hanc publicam causam conferre. Porro autem haud prorsus simili argumento eundem titulum inscripsi, quem adversus Pelagianos fecit Aug. Ille enim in libro de natura et gratia^[*Argumentum.*] imbecillitatem duntaxat, inopiamque intendebat demonstrare laesi, vulneratique liberi arbitrii: cui proinde necessaria omnino esset gratia CHRISTI, Ego vero Reverendissimi antistites, quo quintae sextaeque consultissimis sessionibus vestris, quae sunt de originali peccato, et de iustificatione, ceu quandam apologiam circumscriberem, altius rem statui repetere, et proferre latius. Ita enim controversias, quae nobis cum Lutheranis sunt, explicatius disserum iri iudicaui, si non eas praecise, verum et materias universas, quae quoquo pacto huic negotio inservire possunt, ex ordine tractare. Nempe si in universum disquirerem, quid in officiis humanis natura nostra cum generali influentia Dei efficere valeat: quidque deinde sit, quod absque speciali favore et auxilio gratiae nequeat. Idcirco naturam nostram in quatuor status et habitus distinguendam duxi. Sane ut hominem in puris naturalibus mente excogitam, in originali iustitia revera conditum, in culpam inde collapsum, ac denique in gratiam postea restitutum depingerem. Sed tam in tres affines libellos^[*Distributio.*] distributio est operis. Quorum primo, qui est de transgressione hominis, tres priores status expedivimus. In altero qui est de iustificatione, causas universas, ac denique modos reconciliationis humanae elucidavimus. In tertio denique de facultate iustificati hominis et certitudine gratiae postremas disputationes adiecimus. Ut primus sit veluti quintae sessionis commentarius: reliqui vero, sextae. His namque deliberatis, pleniter intelligere possumus, et unde fuerit homo suo libero arbitrio deiectus, et quo fuerit deinceps divina gratia revocatus. Ceterum stylo et ratione procedendi ac disserendi non admodum sumus scholasticam formam aspernati,^[*Stylus scholasticus non est aspernandus.*] Tametsi haud nesciam, quod sit scholasticorum nomen Lutheranis inuisum et infame.^[*Lutheranorum vafricies.*] Nam quid non inde isti ab initio designarunt, ex quo bellum hoc Ecclesiae inferre coeprunt? Porro ut quosque hominum ordines plurimum metuebant, ita eosdem, quo eorum adversus se auctoritatem defingerent, maximis coeperunt insectari odiis, convitiis proscindere, et maledictis acerrime incessere: atque ideo quasi suspectos hostes e suis colloquiis congressibusque abigere. Hac de causa scholasticos theologos, velut publicam perniciem exibilant. Quoniam, ut in fabula est Demosthenis, non possunt pecuarii canes,^[*Scholastica Theologia immerito abiicitur.*] quod gregis sint propugnatores, non esse lupis invisi. Atqui si superis placet, acsi essent ipsi, qui iura deberent ponere orbi, ita sunt inter catholicos multi, qui eos audientes, quaestionarios posthabent, philosophiam abiiciunt, et solis volunt linguarum ferculis conuiuium instrui: utpote quarum cognitione et subsidio arbitrantur absque Theseo per se posse, cum sanctorum Patrum, tum etiam sacrae paginae adire volumina. Cui profecto malo (id quod coram vestra sanctitate in publica synodo declamavi) nisi obviam publicitus occurratis, et universitates melius sibi et bono publico consultum properent, totum brevi Christianum orbem errores ebullire dolebimus. Quid ni? Ut quisque impensissime studet trilinguis euadere, tanquam fabuloso illo fonte prolusset labra, ita maxima auctoritate inter sacrorum mystas Trimegistus prodit. Nihil sane est, quod huic meae infacundiae praetexere velim. Nanque et ingenue fateor alia me ratione studia instituisse, quod ut linguas accuratissime excolerem: et si alterum optandum foret, mallem in praesentiarum spiritum Christiano propinquum, quod eloquentiam Ciceronianae proximam mihi dari. Neque vero diffiteor linguarum peritiam et cultum, cui nostro aeuo diligentius incumbitur, sacris intelligendis bibliis magno usui esse:^[*Linguarum peritia necessaria. Schol.theolog. repuganda.*] id cuius nos. 2. de doct. Chri. admonet Aug. Verum hoc tamen vicissim persuasum contendo, quod uti oculus ophthalmia laborans non protinus cerebro eruitur, sed collyriis propter eius optimam usuram curatur: ita sit res scholastica amputanda, nempe et a sophismatum quidem nugis, et a metaphysicorum vanis portentis repurganda, quibus est sordibus apud nonnullos auctores indigne foedata: detur tamen summa opera, ne penitus depereat, sed instauretur potius, nisi plurimus volumus, habere nomen: rarissimos tamen, re esse theologos. Non adeo expressa extat in S. Patribus ratio haec per quaestiones disputandi: at cum fuerint summi philosophi^[*Patres philosophiam docti fuerunt.*] planum est peripateticam hanc formam novisse. Quae sane quanuis non erat inter enarranda eloquia sacra necessaria, nihilominus apud Augu. et alios crebro se exerit. Et quando post illam aetatem fuisset in scholas theologorum recepta, ecquid eius negotium est, si via, ratione, et modo instituatur, nisi ut fides per hanc artem salubrissima (quod ait. 14. de trini. Aug.)^[*Aug. 14. de trini.*] gignatur, nutriatur, defendatur et roboretur? Nam quae potest perspicacior esse, commodiorque ratio interpretandi, cum sanctorum dicta, tum maxime sacrorum eloquia, quod dum locus unus in quaestionem mittitur: unde materia subiecta ex suis causis explicata, verus depromitur sensus? Veluti est apud S. Thomam, S. Bonaventuram et reliquos perspicere. Est enim homo rationale animal,^[*Homini ingenita est ratiocinatio.*] qui nulla idcirco vi magis, viaque pollet, ad eruendam undecunque veritatem, atque ex suis causis deducendam, quod ratiocinatione et discursu. Atque adeo, ut rerum causas naturasque disquirat, consequentia iudicet, conciliet contraria, incognitum denique quidvis ex penitissimis latebris in lucem prodat, nulla re magis adiuvatur, quod congressibus, si ordine fiant, ceterisque scholasticis exercitiis. Adde quod naturam fides, non (uti isti autumant) adversatur: sed certe perficit.^[*Fides naturae perfectio.*] Quapropter vicaria se luce mutuo perfundunt. Nempe ut plurima nos fides erudivit naturae secreta philosophis ante inaccessa, sic vicissim et intelligendis explicandisque mysteriis fidei plurimum cognitio rerum naturalium ancillatur. Eo potissimum, quod praeter illa divinorum arcana, cetera omnia, nempe quae ad leges, quae ad virtutes et vitia, quae ad officia humana, contractus, necessitudinesque hominum attinent (quae sunt cuncta in Republica Christiana cognitu maxime necessaria) soli sunt scholastici, a quibus discutiuntur et pertractantur. Quorum rationes magna ex parte philosophia subministrat. Sed aiunt philosophorum semper scholas haeresum fuisse officinas.^[*Philosophia quandoque nocet, sed rursus prodest.*] Haud equidem diffiteor, dum fides in cunabulis infantiam agebat. Tunc enim quae res erat supra, easdem scioli contra naturam iudicabant. Hinc Arrius, Sabellius, et id genus monstra prodiere. Hac de causa apud priscos orthodoxos male audit philosophia. Attamen nisi fuissent inter eos, qui philosophos ex ipsa etiam philosophia evincerent, vix beluas illas sacris testimoniis, quae in sinistrum sensum ab illis detorquebantur, superassent. Philosophos enim fuisse necesse erat, qui explicarent, ut non esset demonstratio, quam Arrius invictissimam censebatur. Nempe quod si individua essentia est pater, eademque filius, pater sit persona filii. A philosophia falsus fuit Berengarius, qui negabat accidentia sacramenti esse sine subiecto, quia repugnare hallucinabatur ipsi eorum naturae: quo nunc etiam Germanorum permulti tenentur errore. Sed vera philosophia est, quae edocet minime id repugnare. Si fieri posset, ut nulli essent pseudophilosophi, qui haereses progignerent, nulla forte in hunc usum necessaria esset philosophia, quae haereticorum ausum retunderet. Verum quod est (auctore Paulo) necesse haereses esse,^[*1. Cor. 11.*] tam necessarium existimaverim, philosophiam inter theologos confovendam esse, qua sint, iuxta verbum Petri, paratiores ad satisfactionem omni poscenti rationem de ea quae in nobis est spe.^[*1. Pet. 3.*] Est enim naturalis philosophiae munus,^[*Philosophiae munus.*] supernaturalia fidei mysteria, non quidem demonstrare (quippe quae ex solis sint divinis testimoniis recepta) sed tamen explicare, et contra philosophos asserere: dum eorum eneruat defringitque argumenta: ostendens, nihil adversus nos euincere. Unde et Paulus episcopum admonet,^[*Tit. 1.*] ut fidelem habeat sermonem, quo potens sit exhortari doctrina sana, et eos, qui contradicunt, arguere. Et sane Aug. quanto sua dialectica et philosophia maius exhibuit Ecclesiae negotium, dum erat Manichaeus, tanto fuit ei postea adversus haereticos utilior. Theriaca philosophia caeleste circumspectissime senatus, quae earundem medetur viperarum morsibus, ex quarum conficitur carnibus.^[*Philosophia theriacae comparatur. Quae fuerit causa Lutheranis errandi.*] Et ut semel finis, quinam linguas, quod Germani excultius posuere? Qui Augustino et id genus Patribus legendis plus temporis insumpserunt? Qui plures sacram paginam reuoluerunt? Quid ergo restat illis causae tam plurium errorum, quod quod theologiam scholasticam neglexerint? Ex cuius ignorantia omnes dimanasse, facile erit rem perpendenti conspicere. Profecto simul, apud eosdemque coepere, et linguarum cultura, et scholasticae rationis contemptus, et haeresum turba. Nescio viri Patres, quo me longius, quod putaram, surripuerit dicendi calor. Boni tamen pro vestra clementia consulite: quoniam paucioribus effari nequivi, scholasticis tractationibus de medio sublatis, quod rei timeam theologicae. Ne vos tamen viri sacri hac mea inepta proloquendi prolixitate diutius obtundam, hoc qualecunque munusculum accipite, perspicite, castigate, et pro summa auctoritate vestra reformate. Nam cui alii quam vobis Ecclesiae lumina, vestrorum apologiam decretorum nuncuparem? Agite ut coepistis. Obsequimini spiritui sancto. Honori apostolicae sedis, ubi sanctissimum Ecclesiae caput residet, consulite. Familiae vestrae, Christiano inquam orbi, sanguine CHRISTI servato, prospicite: qui intenta in vos ora tenet, expansasque manus: ut hanc, quae reliqua est, fidei scintillam excitetis, Christianos principes audite, hoc a vobis obnixe flagitantes, qui de hac causa sedetis iudices, zelus, officiumque invictissimi^[*Zelus Caesaris.*] Caesaris haud per vos sanctissimo suo sine defraudetur. Qui non modo in hanc eandem causam, fortunas omnes, exercitus, regna utique exposuit, sed quo fidem suam, quam CHRISTO obstrinxerat, liberaret, vitam in castris, prodigiosis armis, iaculis utique sulphureis: obiecit: ut sit eius fama ad gloriam divini nominis, sempiterna. Namque si hoc loco Christianam Rempublicam relinquitis, cum neque fides in tanto periculo durare diu, neque mundus ea extincta, possit esse superstes, in timorem nos certum coniicitis, ne haec tam late patens discessio ea sit ipsa, de qua scriptum nobis curavit Apostolus, praenuntiam fore appropinquantis rerum finis.

texts.content: Would that, holy, ecumenical, and in every way legitimate Synod of Trent, this fire stirred up from the North had not invaded the Church of God more violently and dangerously than [a fire] which it is now easy to resist. For I would not then have rushed so rashly into public, until I had weighed my own poverty with myself, consulted my weakness, and found out what my shoulders could bear. But when we, astonished, see that the world of Christians is now ablaze from so many quarters,^[*The Lutheran fire spreads far and wide.*] and that so many sparks have leaped from it that scarcely any corner remains which does not already smoke, about to catch the flame, I have indeed thought nothing else worth the effort, if each man, according to his strength and the talent divinely given him, hastens without choice to meet it in some improvised way, and we all bring help, so that if in some part it has already eaten into men’s marrow and reduced their hearts to ashes, and we cannot extinguish it, at least it may not continue to flash and sparkle more widely—that is, in fine, our effort. We especially who have been brought here to write on this matter. For to this purpose Caesar also sent my smallness to you, most holy Fathers, if perhaps I could render you any service whatsoever. But if all were obedient to the word of this sacred order, as Christians are bound in the highest right, they would surely have enough to have heard your most holy counsels, and to obey them obediently. For what is there that can be objected to an ecumenical council, legitimately both summoned and assembled? Where, according to the Holy Spirit, three most reverend legates from the chief men of the sacred senate preside, worthy indeed to discharge the office of Vicar of Christ. With whom also two other Cardinals of the same order, both most distinguished and most wise, sit as assessors. Where the princes of Christians have sent their envoys along with holy bishops. Where finally from all lands the most just and most prudent number of every rank and ecclesiastical dignity has been gathered. But among the errors of that Patriarch Luther there is this one,^[*Luther’s error.*] the cause and fuel of all, and by far the most pestilent of all: that he admits no public judge for defining and terminating controversies of faith, whose authority and judgment all Christians should obey. And this has so settled into the minds of those Lutherans that, after thirty years spent in truces, assemblies and conferences with them, they have now despaired of preparing their minds beforehand for the council, and have taken up unspeakable arms^[*The arms of the Lutherans.*] against the sacred Majesty, the parent of his country, against the Church of God, against the truth of the Gospel. See, alas, most excellent Fathers, whither the obstinate blindness of one man has finally come. And what is greater and a more grievous marvel, never have any errors, so slight and slender, whether you look to holiness of life or to doctrine, had progenitors and patrons.^[*The Lutherans are not so powerful.*] For they are not even covered with a sheep’s skin, nor much instructed in art. And yet never have any been more destructive to the Christian commonwealth, never have any spread so widely with less effort, and so seized the minds not only of the unlearned crowd but of the nobles and princes of the Germans—a race truly most celebrated throughout the whole world for its illustrious deeds, and also, had it not received this blow, most Christian in the sanctity of its religion. But is it not a miracle where the natural cause is so ready to hand?^[*The causes of heresies.*] They teach that whatever pleases is lawful. But I have resolved to admonish my brothers, not to provoke them; for charity does not act perversely. All whom Christ has regenerated with me in the same blood I embrace with the same charity. I congratulate some on recognizing the evangelical truth; for others I desire that they may no longer ignore it, and I pray the immortal God for it. Especially since I wish that our own corrupted morals and the dissipation of laws had not been the occasion these men seized for so great a separation. For whatever it was that drove the ship of Peter into these rocks, it was the storm of our own evils. And unless we take care that this be first calmed, you strive in vain, most ample Fathers, to settle the disturbance of affairs which we suffer, and to check the waves of heresies by which we are tossed. Yet the adversaries could have censured the errors of persons without injury to the public faith. For whatever the morals of private men and the abuses of laws may be, the truth of faith is nevertheless beyond all doubt true. For it is divine, and so firm and holy that to oppose it out of any hatred or pretext is a nefarious crime of impiety. Wherefore, to return to the beginning from which I digressed: I have by no means received five talents, nor indeed two, which I might be able to double further at interest (according to the Gospel); but so great has the necessity of these times seemed to me that a little fear has begun to move me somewhat, lest perhaps even the one which I have received according to my slender strength I now bury in the earth, and that be reckoned to me as wickedness on the day of the Lord. For this reason, after so many and such illustrious men who in these thirty years have happily contended with them on our side, I have prepared this little work On Nature and Grace,^[*The name of the work.*] meditating whether perhaps my labor might avail to contribute something to this public cause. Moreover, I have not given it altogether a similar argument to the same title which Augustine wrote against the Pelagians. For he in the book On Nature and Grace^[*The argument.*] intended only to demonstrate the weakness and poverty of wounded and injured free will, for which therefore the grace of Christ was altogether necessary. But I, most Reverend bishops, so as to set forth as it were a kind of apology for your most prudent fifth and sixth sessions, which are on original sin and on justification, have decided to repeat the matter from a higher source and to set it forth more broadly. For thus I judged that the controversies which we have with the Lutherans would be explained more clearly if I treated in order not precisely those controversies, but all the matters which can in any way serve this business. Namely, if I inquired universally what our nature in human offices can accomplish with the general influence of God, and what then it is that it cannot do without the special favor and help of grace. Therefore I have thought our nature should be distinguished into four states and conditions: namely, that I should depict man as conceived in thought in pure natural state, as truly created in original justice, as fallen from there into fault, and finally as afterward restored to grace. But the distribution of the work is into three related little books.^[*Distribution.*] In the first of these, which is on the transgression of man, we have dispatched the first three states. In the second, which is on justification, we have elucidated all the causes and finally the modes of human reconciliation. In the third, finally, we have added the last disputations on the faculty of the justified man and the certainty of grace. So that the first may be as it were a commentary on the fifth session, and the rest on the sixth. For with these things deliberated, we can fully understand both whence man was cast down by his free will and whither he was afterward recalled by divine grace. Moreover, in style and in the manner of proceeding and disputing, I have not much rejected the scholastic form,^[*The scholastic style is not to be rejected.*] although I am not unaware that the name of the Scholastics is hateful and infamous to the Lutherans.^[*The cunning of the Lutherans.*] For what did these men not designate from the beginning, from the time they began to wage this war against the Church? Moreover, as they feared every order of men the most, so, in order to disparage their authority against themselves, they began to attack them with the greatest hatred, to tear them with insults, and to assail them most bitterly with curses—and therefore to drive them from their conferences and assemblies as suspected enemies. For this reason they hiss out the scholastic theologians as a public pestilence. Because, as in Demosthenes’ fable, the herdsmen’s dogs^[*Scholastic theology is undeservedly cast away.*] cannot, since they are the defenders of the flock, be not hateful to wolves. But if it please the gods, as if they themselves were the ones who ought to lay down laws for the world, so there are many among Catholics who, listening to them, put the schoolmen last, cast aside philosophy, and wish the banquet to be furnished with the dishes of languages alone, since by their knowledge and assistance they think that without a Theseus they can of themselves approach both the volumes of the holy Fathers and also of sacred Scripture. To this evil, certainly (as I declaimed before your holiness in the public synod), unless you publicly resist, and the universities hasten to consult better for themselves and for the public good, we shall soon grieve that the whole Christian world boils over with errors. Why not? As each man most impudently strives to become trilingual and has washed his lips at that fabulous fountain, so he comes forth with the greatest authority among the priests of the sacred mysteries, a very Thrice-great. There is nothing indeed that I wish to pretend in excuse of my lack of eloquence. For I frankly confess that I have pursued studies for another reason—namely, that I might cultivate languages most accurately; and if the other were to be desired, I would rather at present have a spirit near to the Christian [matter] than that eloquence nearest to Cicero be given me. Nor do I deny that the knowledge and cultivation of languages, to which our age applies itself more diligently, is of great use for understanding the sacred books:^[*Knowledge of languages is necessary. Scholastic theology is to be defended.*] Augustine reminds us of this in On Christian Doctrine 2. But nevertheless I contend, on the other hand, that this should be persuaded: that as an eye suffering from ophthalmia is not immediately torn from the head, but is cured with eye-salves for the sake of its excellent use, so the scholastic matter should be cut away—namely, purged both of the trifles of sophisms and of the vain monstrosities of the metaphysicians, with which it has been unworthily defiled by the filth of some authors—yet the greatest effort should be given that it not utterly perish, but rather be restored, unless we wish to have very many who bear the name, but very few who in reality are theologians. Not so expressly does this method of disputing through questions exist in the holy Fathers; but since they were the greatest philosophers,^[*The Fathers were learned in philosophy.*] it is plain that they knew this Peripatetic form. And although it was not necessary among the narratives of the sacred utterances, it nevertheless frequently shows itself in Augustine and others. And since after that age it was received into the schools of the theologians, what is its business, if it is instituted by the way, reason and method, except that faith through this most healthful art (as Augustine says in On the Trinity 14)^[*Augustine, On the Trinity 14.*] may be begotten, nourished, defended and strengthened? For what method of interpreting can be more perspicacious and more suitable, both for the sayings of the saints and especially for the utterances of the sacred writers, than that, when one passage is brought into question, the underlying matter, explained from its causes, may yield the true sense? As it is to be seen in Saint Thomas, Saint Bonaventure and the rest. For man is a rational animal,^[*Reasoning is innate to man.*] and therefore by no power does he prevail more, or by any way, for drawing out truth from every source and deducing it from its causes, than by reasoning and discourse. And so, in order to investigate the causes and natures of things, to judge consequences, to reconcile contraries, and finally to bring forth anything unknown from its deepest hiding places into the light, he is aided by nothing more than by conferences, if they are conducted in order, and the other scholastic exercises. Add that faith does not oppose nature (as these men think), but certainly perfects it.^[*Faith is the perfection of nature.*] Wherefore they mutually pour themselves into each other with a borrowed light. For as faith has taught us very many secrets of nature previously inaccessible to philosophers, so in turn the knowledge of natural things greatly serves as a handmaid for understanding and explaining the mysteries of faith. Especially since, besides those hidden things of divine matters, all other things—namely, those which pertain to laws, to virtues and vices, to human offices, contracts, and the relationships of men (all of which are most necessary to be known in a Christian commonwealth)—are discussed and treated by the Scholastics alone, whose reasons philosophy supplies in large part. But they say that the schools of the philosophers have always been the workshops of heresies.^[*Philosophy sometimes harms, but again it helps.*] I do not deny that this was so while faith was in its infancy in the cradle. For then those who thought themselves wise judged the things that were above them against nature. Hence Arius, Sabellius, and monsters of that kind came forth. For this reason philosophy has a bad name among the early orthodox. Yet unless there had been among them those who would conquer the philosophers even from philosophy itself, they would scarcely have overcome those beasts by the sacred testimonies which those men twisted into a sinister sense. For there had to be philosophers to explain that it was not a demonstration which Arius was thought to have most invincibly—namely, that if the individual essence is the Father, and the same is the Son, then the Father is the person of the Son. Berengar was refuted by philosophy, who denied that the accidents of the sacrament exist without a subject, because he hallucinated that this was repugnant to their very nature; and in that error many Germans are now held. But true philosophy is that which teaches that this is in no way repugnant. If it could be brought about that there were no false philosophers to beget heresies, perhaps no philosophy would be necessary for this use, to blunt the audacity of heretics. But because (according to Paul) there must be heresies,^[*1 Corinthians 11.*] I would have judged it equally necessary that philosophy be cherished among theologians, by which, according to Peter’s word, they may be more ready to give a reason to everyone who asks about the hope that is in us.^[*1 Peter 3.*] For it is the office of natural philosophy^[*The office of philosophy.*] not indeed to demonstrate the supernatural mysteries of faith (since they are received from divine testimonies alone), but nevertheless to explain them and to assert them against the philosophers, while it weakens and breaks their arguments, showing that they prove nothing against us. Hence Paul also admonishes the bishop^[*Titus 1.*] to hold to the faithful word, so that he may be able to exhort by sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict. And indeed, the more Augustine exhibited the business of the Church by his dialectic and philosophy while he was a Manichaean, the more useful he afterward was against heretics. Philosophy is a theriac, a heavenly remedy most carefully provided by the senate, which cures the bites of the very vipers from whose flesh it is made.^[*Philosophy is compared to theriac. What was the cause of the Lutherans’ erring.*] And to make an end at once: who are they who have set languages in a more cultivated way than the Germans? Who have spent more time in reading Augustine and the Fathers of that kind? Who have turned over more copies of sacred Scripture? What cause, then, remains to them for so many errors, except that they have neglected scholastic theology? From ignorance of it that all have flowed, it will be easy for one who weighs the matter to perceive. Indeed, among the same men there began at once both the cultivation of languages and contempt for scholastic reasoning, and a crowd of heresies. I know not, Fathers, whither the heat of speaking has stolen me further than I had thought. But do you, in your clemency, provide for the good, since I could not say in fewer words what I fear for the theological matter if scholastic treatments are removed from the midst. Yet that I may not longer deafen you, holy men, with this inept prolixity of my speaking, receive this little gift, whatever it is, examine it, chastise it, and reform it according to your supreme authority. For to whom other than you, the lights of the Church, should I dedicate the apology of your decrees? Act as you have begun. Be obedient to the Holy Spirit. Consult the honor of the apostolic see, where the most holy head of the Church resides. Provide for your family—I mean the Christian world—kept by the blood of Christ, which holds its faces fixed upon you and its hands outstretched, that you may stir up this remaining spark of faith; hear the Christian princes, who earnestly beg this of you, who sit as judges in this cause: let not the zeal and office of the most invincible Caesar^[*The zeal of Caesar.*] be defrauded through you of its most holy purpose. He has exposed not only all his fortunes, armies and kingdoms to this same cause, but also, that he might discharge the faith he had bound himself to Christ, he has set his life before you in the camp, with prodigious arms and indeed with sulphurous missiles, so that his fame may be eternal to the glory of the divine name. For if you leave the Christian commonwealth at this point, when faith cannot long endure in so great a danger, and the world cannot survive once it is extinguished, you cast us into certain fear that this departure, spreading so widely, is that very one about which the Apostle took care to write to us, foretelling the approaching end of things.
